theme: Pressing on; contentment; the peace of God
readingInstruction: Read Philippians 3:1-4:23. Paul gives his own testimony, speaks of pressing on, and ends with practical commands about joy, prayer, peace, and contentment. Read 3:7-14 and 4:4-13 slowly.
settingTheScene: In chapter 3, Paul warns the Philippians against those who trust in the flesh, including Judaizers who insisted on circumcision. He offers his own credentials and shows why he counts them as rubbish. Chapter 4 begins with a plea for two women in the church to be reconciled, followed by the best-known statements on joy, anxiety, and contentment. Paul wrote this in prison, which gives the commands special force.
observation: “Indeed, I count everything as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord” (3:8).
“That I may know him and the power of his resurrection, and may share his sufferings, becoming like him in his death” (3:10).
“I press on toward the goal for the prize of the upward call of God in Christ Jesus” (3:14).
“Rejoice in the Lord always; again I will say, Rejoice” (4:4).
“Do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God” (4:6).
“Whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just” (4:8).
“I have learned in whatever situation I am to be content” (4:11).
“I can do all things through him who strengthens me” (4:13).
interpretation:
Paul begins with a warning: “Look out for the dogs, look out for the evildoers, look out for those who mutilate the flesh. For we are the circumcision, who worship by the Spirit of God and glory in Christ Jesus and put no confidence in the flesh.” He then lists his own credentials: circumcised on the eighth day, of the people of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews, a Pharisee, a persecutor of the church, as to righteousness under the law blameless. “But whatever gain I had, I counted as loss for the sake of Christ. Indeed, I count everything as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord. For his sake I have suffered the loss of all things and count them as rubbish, in order that I may gain Christ and be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but that which comes through faith in Christ, the righteousness from God that depends on faith.” This is the gospel from his own heart.

The goal is to know Christ: “that I may know him and the power of his resurrection, and may share his sufferings, becoming like him in his death, that by any means possible I may attain the resurrection from the dead.” Paul has not yet arrived. “Brothers, I do not consider that I have made it my own. But one thing I do: forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead, I press on toward the goal for the prize of the upward call of God in Christ Jesus.” Like a runner, he keeps his eyes on the finish. He calls the mature to share this mindset and to imitate him. “But our citizenship is in heaven, and from it we await a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body.”

Chapter 4 opens with a plea. Euodia and Syntyche, two women who labored beside Paul in the gospel, should agree in the Lord. Then the famous passage: “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I will say, Rejoice. Let your reasonableness be known to everyone. The Lord is at hand; do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.” Anxiety is replaced by prayer, and the result is peace that stands guard. Paul then directs the mind: “Whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is commendable, if there is any excellence, if there is anything worthy of praise, think about these things.”

He thanks them for their gift and reveals the secret of contentment: “I have learned in whatever situation I am to be content. I know how to be brought low, and I know how to abound. In any and every circumstance, I have learned the secret of facing plenty and hunger, abundance and need.” The secret: “I can do all things through him who strengthens me.” This verse is often misused as a promise of success in every endeavor. In context, it means Christ gives strength to endure any circumstance, whether abundance or need. He closes with a promise: “My God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus.”
connection: Romans 3:21-26 and Galatians 2:15-21 expand on a righteousness from God by faith. 1 Corinthians 9:24-27 and 2 Timothy 4:7 also use the race image. Colossians 3:1-4 speaks of citizenship and the heavenly life. Matthew 6:25-34 teaches not to be anxious. 1 Peter 5:7 says to cast all your anxieties on him. 1 Timothy 6:6-10 speaks of godliness with contentment. Hebrews 13:5 says be content with what you have. 2 Corinthians 12:9-10 gives Christ’s strength in weakness. Isaiah 26:3 promises perfect peace.
application:
When anxiety comes, turn each worry into a specific prayer with thanksgiving.

Think on the list of verse 8 for ten minutes. Write down things that fit each description.

Ask what you need to count as loss for the sake of knowing Christ.
prayerPrompts: Tell Jesus that you count everything as loss compared to knowing him.
Ask him to help you press on toward the goal.
Give him your anxieties with thanksgiving.
